title: SRE SLOs, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing and internal inference services (hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane).
- Covers SLO definitions, error budget policy and burn controls, capacity planning processes, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook expectations.

Purpose
This document codifies Redwood Inference SRE expectations and processes so teams can:
1) Define measurable SLOs and manage error budgets consistently.
2) Plan capacity to meet availability and latency targets while controlling cost.
3) Run blameless incident reviews and track reliability improvements.
4) Maintain operational tooling and runbooks that allow on-call engineers to troubleshoot and mitigate incidents quickly.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
- Definitions and conventions:
  - SLI (Service Level Indicator): a measured metric representing customer experience (examples: 95th percentile request latency, successful request ratio, embedding freshness).
  - SLO (Service Level Objective): target on an SLI over a rolling time window (typically 30d and 90d).
  - Error budget: 1 - SLO; amount of allowable unreliability used to authorize changes and rollouts.

- Standard SLO tiers (default targets used across most inference services):
  | Tier | Availability SLO (success rate) | Latency SLO (p95) | Measurement window |
  |------|-------------------------------:|------------------:|-------------------:|
  | Gold | 99.95%                        | <= 250 ms         | 30d / 90d          |
  | Silver | 99.9%                       | <= 400 ms         | 30d / 90d          |
  | Bronze | 99.5%                       | <= 800 ms         | 30d / 90d          |

- Service-specific SLOs:
  - Each service owner must publish SLOs in the service's Confluence page and register SLIs in our monitoring catalog (Prometheus/Cortex).
  - Example SLO entries to publish: metric name, prometheus query, alerting thresholds, owner, SLO tier, measurement windows.

- Error budget policy and burn actions:
  - Low burn (<= 25% of budget used in 30d): normal operations; teams may proceed with standard deploys.
  - Medium burn (25% < burn <= 50%): engineering lead review; schedule immediate reliability check; postpone risky rollouts.
  - High burn (50% < burn <= 75%): mandatory reliability review; freeze non-critical rollouts until mitigations are in place.
  - Critical burn (> 75%): emergency response; rollback recent changes, reduce traffic via routing policy, engage SRE on-call for deep investigation.

2) Measurement and Tooling
- Monitoring and metrics stack:
  - Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long term storage.
  - Traces: OpenTelemetry -> Tempo.
  - Logs: Loki for structured logs; Datadog as secondary aggregation for business metrics.
  - Error budget dashboard: Grafana dashboard per service showing SLO, burn rate, and attribution of failures by error class.

- Measurement rules:
  - SLIs must be computed from production ingress (edge/proxy) where possible to capture end-to-end user experience.
  - Synthetic checks may be used only to augment SLIs, not replace production-derived SLIs.
  - Aggregation windows: compute 30d rolling and 90d rolling SLO windows; surface both on dashboards.

3) Capacity Planning
- Objectives:
  - Ensure capacity to meet SLOs during normal and peak demand while minimizing reserved costs.
  - Maintain a safety buffer (headroom) to absorb traffic spikes and noisy neighbors.

- Quarterly capacity planning cadence:
  1. Forecast demand using historical telemetry (QPS, token/sec, request size distribution) and expected product launches.
  2. Convert demand to infrastructure units (GPU-hours, vCPU, memory) using service-specific efficiency profiles.
  3. Define provisioning plan: baseline reserved capacity + burst capacity policy.
  4. Execute procurement or scaling configs (Dedicated pool resizing, autoscaling policy changes).
  5. Post-provision validation: run synthetic load tests and smoke tests.

- Headroom targets (defaults):
  - Hosted API critical paths: 25% headroom across p95 expected load.
  - Dedicated customer pools: 15% headroom unless contract specifies otherwise.
  - Private deployments: align with customer SLA; include explicit sizing worksheet in the customer Confluence folder.

- Autoscaling and burst policies:
  - Use multi-dimensional autoscaling (QPS, GPU utilization, queue length).
  - Configure cooldowns and max burst caps to avoid thrash.
  - During capacity shortages, use smart routing policies: route to compatible model variants or lower-tier pools before shedding requests.

4) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization
- Program structure:
  - Each quarter SRE and product agree on 2-3 reliability OKRs (e.g., reduce p99 tail latency by 20% for chat endpoints, reduce mean time to mitigate P1s to < 20 minutes).
  - Initiatives are tracked in the reliability board with owner, success criteria, and milestones.

- Typical initiative categories:
  - Observability improvements (SLI coverage, dashboards, alert tuning).
  - Capacity & autoscaling improvements (efficient batching, eviction policies).
  - Runtime performance (kernel selection, quantization profiles, KV caching).
  - Operational tooling (improved runbooks, playbooks, chaos testing).

5) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)
- Principles:
  - Blameless, timely, and action-oriented.
  - Prioritize learning and measurable follow-ups.

- Postmortem template (required fields):
  1. Incident summary (one-paragraph): impact, duration, customers affected.
  2. Timeline of events (timestamped).
  3. Root cause analysis (technical and organizational).
  4. Immediate mitigations and rollbacks performed.
  5. Long-term fixes and owners (with due dates).
  6. Action items (measurable, assigned, due date).
  7. Severity classification and whether SLA was breached.
  8. Follow-up review date.

- Review cadence and distribution:
  - P1 and P0 incidents: postmortem published within 72 hours; review meeting within 7 days with stakeholders.
  - P2: postmortem within 7 days.
  - All postmortems are posted to eng-sre incident repository and linked to the product incident tracker.

- Example severity mapping:
  - P0: System-wide outage affecting >50% customers or critical business flows.
  - P1: Major degradation affecting important customer subsets or critical SLAs.
  - P2: Partial degradation with no immediate SLA breach.

6) Operational Tooling and On-call
- On-call structure:
  - Primary SRE on-call (24/7 rotation) for threshold breaches and major incidents.
  - Secondary/secondary support for escalation and deep-dive.
  - Pager duty runbook: schedule, escalation policy, phone tree.

- Tooling inventory (primary tools and owner):
  - PagerDuty (alerts and escalation) - owner: eng-sre ops.
  - Grafana + Alertmanager (SLO dashboards and alerts) - owner: eng-platform.
  - Prometheus/Cortex (metrics) - owner: eng-infra.
  - Loki (logs) - owner: eng-platform.
  - OpenTelemetry + Tempo (traces) - owner: eng-serving-runtime.
  - Runbook library (Confluence + playbook links) - owner: eng-sre.

- Alerting guidance:
  - Alert on symptoms, not implementation details (e.g., "inference-p95 > 500ms" not "worker-123 reporting slow loop").
  - Configure deduplication, grouping, and runbook links on each alert.
  - Use severity aligned to SLO impact; map to on-call paging thresholds.

7) Runbooks: Standards and Examples
- Runbook structure (required sections):
  - Title and short description
  - Owner and escalation contacts
  - Symptoms and detection (SLIs/alert names)
  - Immediate mitigation steps (numbered)
  - Diagnostic commands and queries (copyable)
  - Rollback and recovery steps
  - Post-incident checks and monitoring validation
  - Related pages and runbook version history

- Example runbook: model-serving-api-high-latency
  - Owner: platform-sre@redwood.ai
  - Symptoms: grafana alert "model-serving-api_p95_latency_high" fires; p95 > 400ms for 5m.
  - Immediate mitigation steps:
    1) Check global error budget dashboard and recent deploys.
    2) Scale replica count for the model-serving pods by +30% (kubectl patch deployment ... or runbook CLI).
    3) If latency persists, enable degraded routing to lower-capacity model variants: run "/ops/routing switch --service model-serving --variant model-small --weight 20%".
    4) If errors increase, rollback the most recent deploy: run "deployctl rollback --service model-serving --count 1".
  - Diagnostic commands (examples):
    - Prometheus query: rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="model-serving"}[5m])
    - kubectl top pods -l app=model-serving --namespace=prod
    - tail logs: kubectl logs -l app=model-serving -n prod --since=15m | grep ERROR | tail -n 200

- Runbook maintenance:
  - Owners must review runbooks quarterly and after any incident where the runbook was used.
  - Runbooks must include a version and last-validated timestamp.

8) Governance and Ownership
- SLO ownership:
  - Each service has a designated SLO owner (usually the service product/engineering lead) responsible for publishing SLOs, defining customer impact classes, and ensuring instrumentation.
  - SRE owns the error budget policy, tooling, and enforcement guidance.

- Approval and change control:
  - Any change to a Gold-tier SLO requires review by Eng SRE leads and sign-off from Product.
  - Changes to capacity plans that affect customer commitments (Dedicated capacity) must be approved by finance + customer success.

9) Reporting and Review
- Weekly reliability digest: automated email summarizing SLO status, top alerting signals, and outstanding action items.
- Quarterly reliability review: presentation to engineering leadership with OKR progress, major incidents, and capacity investments.

Appendices
A. Quick escalation matrix
- PagerDuty Priority -> Primary -> Secondary -> Exec notification
- P0 -> oncall-sre -> infra-lead -> CTO
- P1 -> oncall-sre -> service-owner -> eng-manager

B. Checklist for creating a new service SLO
1) Instrument SLIs at ingress (edge) and export to Prometheus.
2) Write SLO statement and pick tier.
3) Create Grafana dashboard with 30d/90d windows.
4) Add alerting rules for burn-rate and hard thresholds.
5) Publish Confluence page and assign SLO owner.

C. Useful commands and templates
- Postmortem template URL: /confluence/eng-sre/postmortem-template
- Runbook template URL: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-template
- Capacity worksheet template URL: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-sizing-worksheet

Document maintenance
- This page is owned by eng-sre and must be reviewed semi-annually.
- Contact: eng-sre@redwood.ai for questions or suggested updates.
